title: Closures, from scratch
description: Build an intuition for closures by watching one form under your fingertips.

sections.text: A closure is a function bundled together with references to its surrounding state — the lexical environment in which it was declared.
Every function you write in JavaScript is technically a closure. The interesting question is what it closes over.
Capturing a mutable loop variable with var creates a closure over the SAME binding. Use let.
Closures can retain memory. Avoid capturing large DOM nodes in long-lived callbacks.

exercises.title: Implement once()
exercises.brief: Write once(fn) that calls fn only the first time and returns the cached result after.

quiz.question: What does a closure capture?
options: References to variables in the enclosing scope
quiz.explanation: Closures capture live bindings, not snapshotted values.

summary: Closures pair a function with the environment where it was born. Master them and modules, memoization, and hooks click into place.
interviewQuestions: Explain closures to a junior engineer using an example.
How can closures cause memory leaks? How would you audit for them?

title: A mental model for useEffect
description: Effects synchronize your component to external systems — think in terms of setup and cleanup, not lifecycle.

sections.text: Every render, React compares the deps array. If anything changed, it runs cleanup for the old effect and setup for the new one.
Empty deps arrays are almost never what you want when the effect uses props or state.

exercises.title: Room lights
exercises.brief: Sync a Room prop to a chat server: connect on mount, reconnect on prop change, disconnect on unmount.

quiz.question: When does the cleanup function run?
options: Before every re-run of the effect and on unmount
quiz.explanation: Cleanup runs before the next setup and on unmount.

summary: Model effects as synchronization contracts. If you cannot describe the external system, you probably do not need an effect.

resources.label: You might not need an effect

interviewQuestions: When would you avoid useEffect entirely?
What does Strict Mode's double-invocation teach you about your effects?

title: Thinking in axes
description: Once you stop thinking in rows and columns and start thinking in main and cross axes, flex clicks.

sections.text: Flexbox aligns children along a main axis and a cross axis. Change flex-direction and the axes rotate with it.

sections.code:
.row { display: flex; gap: 1rem; align-items: center; }
.push { margin-left: auto; }

exercises.title: Nav bar
exercises.brief: Build a nav bar with a logo, a link cluster, and a right-aligned CTA using only flex.

quiz.question: align-items aligns children along which axis?
quiz.explanation: align-items works on the cross axis; justify-content on the main axis.

summary: Main + cross axis is the whole model. Everything else is defaults and gaps.
interviewQuestions: When would you reach for grid over flex?

title: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR — and now streaming
description: Trade-offs across rendering strategies and the questions that pick the winner.

sections.text: The right rendering strategy is a function of freshness, personalization, cost and TTFB budget.
Ask: who is this page for, how fresh must it be, and can the response be cached at the edge?

exercises.title: Pick a strategy
exercises.brief: Choose a rendering strategy for a marketing home, a logged-in dashboard, and a product page.

quiz.question: Which strategy gives the best TTFB for anonymous, cacheable pages?
quiz.explanation: Prebuilt HTML served from the edge wins TTFB for anonymous cacheable content.

summary: There is no single best. There is a best for this page, right now.
interviewQuestions: Design the rendering strategy for a global e-commerce site.
